Talk about saying goodbye to a place and about a legacy.

It's February 2031. In a week, Mrs Hoffmann is moving into the care home with Friedrich. There's already a piano there. One question remains: what will happen to her Steinway grand piano on the fourth floor?
I've thought about it a lot. Now I have to make a decision. What will happen to my piano?
There's already a piano at the care home, after all. Do you want to sell yours?
Sell it? That's out of the question. This piano has kept me company for sixty years. It mustn't end up with strangers who only use it as a piece of furniture.
May I make a suggestion? At our school there's a music room, but only an old, out-of-tune piano. The children are very interested in music, but they don't have a good instrument.
The primary school on Kastanienallee? Kuba's school?
Exactly. If you made the piano available to the school, twenty children could play it every day. Only if you want to, of course.
Children playing my piano… You know, Jakob, the price doesn't matter. But I have one condition.
The children have to take care of it. No cola on the lid, no chewing gum under the keys. And once a month I'll come and give an hour's lesson. As long as I still can.
Let Mr Wolff know, child. He knows people at the transport company who have strong arms, after all. A grand piano doesn't go down the stairs on its own.

Many ideas can be expressed in German either with a single verb or with a noun + an “empty” verb (treffen, nehmen, stellen, kommen, geben). The noun version is more formal and very common in texts, the news and exams:
to decide / to make a decision
to ask / to ask a question
You can't change the verb! You say “eine Entscheidung treffen”, NOT “eine Entscheidung machen” (even though English says “make a decision”). Learn them as blocks.
2. The most common ones at B1
Sie stellt der Schule den Flügel zur Verfügung.
Ich stehe Ihnen gern zur Verfügung.
Ihr Wunsch ist in Erfüllung gegangen.
“Ich stehe Ihnen gern zur Verfügung” is a classic phrase at the end of a formal email or a cover letter.
3. How to use them in a sentence
The verb is conjugated normally; the noun (with its preposition) usually goes towards the end, like a “bracket”:
Yesterday she finally made a decision.
Today we're saying goodbye to the flat.
…, because she's making her piano available to the school.
She's saying goodbye to the flat.
Please be considerate of the neighbours!
The year is coming to an end.
Die Kinder sollen Rücksicht auf den Flügel nehmen.
The grand piano goes to school

The piano removal took place on a cold Tuesday in February. Mr Wolff had kept his word and brought four colleagues from the transport company, burly men in orange vests who usually repaired tram tracks and were now carrying, with great respect, a black 1958 Steinway down from the fourth floor. It took them two hours, seven breaks and a crate of beer, which Ludwig paid for. Mrs Hoffmann sat down in the courtyard the whole time, in her wheelchair, wrapped in a blanket, and watched. Every time the piano went round a bend, she closed her eyes.

When the piano finally reached the courtyard, on a trolley, under the bare chestnut tree, Mrs Hoffmann asked the men to wait a moment. She wheeled herself over to it, opened the lid and placed her hands on the cold keys. She didn't play anything. She just said goodbye. Sixty years. Thousands of evenings at nine o'clock. Concerts, rehearsals, scales, tears, and in recent years music for a whole courtyard. Then she closed the lid and said: “There. Now it can go. It has done its job in this house.”

The primary school was only three hundred metres away, on the same street. The men from the transport company slowly pushed the piano along the pavement, and behind them walked a small procession: Mrs Hoffmann in her wheelchair, pushed by Mara, Ludwig with Fritz, Lena and Andrei with a flask, Jakob at the front. Passers-by stopped and watched. An old man took off his hat. A young mother with a pram asked what was going on. “A grand piano is going to school,” said Ludwig. The young mother didn't understand, but she smiled.

At the school, two hundred children were waiting in the assembly hall. Jakob had told them all, and the head teacher had decided there would be no normal lessons that morning. When the piano was pushed through the door, the children clapped so loudly that the windows shook. Kuba was standing in the front row, prouder than ever, explaining to anyone who would listen: “That's the piano from my house. From the fourth floor. I heard it every evening.”

The head teacher, an energetic woman with short grey hair, gave a little speech. She thanked Mrs Hoffmann for making such a valuable instrument available to the school. She said that music plays a big role in education, especially in a school with children from forty countries who don't all speak the same language. “But music,” she said, “everyone understands.”

Then she asked Mrs Hoffmann to play something. Mrs Hoffmann hesitated. Her hands had grown weaker in recent months, and she no longer liked playing in front of strangers. But then she saw the two hundred faces looking at her full of expectation, children from Syria, from Poland, from Vietnam, from Turkey, from Romania, from Berlin, and she made a decision. She let herself be pushed to the piano.
I'm going to play you a song I sang when I was your age. In a cellar, in the war, when we were afraid. If you know it, sing along with me.

She played “Guter Mond, du gehst so stille” (“Good moon, you go so quietly”). Softly, gently, with mistakes. Most of the children didn't know the song. But Kuba knew it, because he had heard it through the wall for years, and he started to sing, loudly and out of tune, like Ludwig. Then Ola sang too. Then a little girl from Syria, who had picked up the melody after two lines. Then Jakob. Then the head teacher. By the end half the hall was singing, and Mrs Hoffmann played the last verse twice, so that everyone could keep up.

Mara was standing at the back, by the wall, and couldn't say a thing. Next to her stood Ludwig, with his glasses in his hand. He didn't wipe them. He simply let the tears run, for the first time, without saying anything about dust.

A week later, Mrs Hoffmann moved into the “Am Kollwitzpark” care home. Her room was on the ground floor, with a door onto the garden, and Friedrich lived next door. In the common room there was a piano, not as beautiful as her Steinway, but tuned. On the first evening they played together, and the other residents, most of them over eighty, came out of their rooms, in dressing gowns and slippers, and sat down quietly on the chairs. Since then, there has been a concert there every evening at nine.

And on the fourth floor of Kastanienallee 31 it was quiet for the first time in sixty years. Mara stood in the courtyard for a long time that evening and looked up at the dark window. Then she heard something. From below, from the second floor, came the melody of “Guter Mond”, played on the cello. Jakob had opened the window. So that the courtyard wouldn't be left without music, he said later. Mara stood in the cold and listened until the song was over.

The next morning, Ludwig knocked on Mara's door, with a bunch of keys in his hand. “Come with me,” was all he said. They went up to the fourth floor together, slowly, step by step, because Ludwig's knees didn't want to any more. The flat was empty. Only the pale patches on the walls showed where pictures had hung for sixty years, and on the wooden floor you could still see the three round marks where the piano had stood. It was the biggest flat in the house, with three rooms, a small balcony overlooking the courtyard and a window through which you could see over the rooftops all the way to the TV tower. Ludwig sat down at that window. “Margarete asked me to find a good tenant,” he said. “Someone who will take care of the flat. And of the music. She said only two people come into question for her.” He turned round and looked at Mara. “A nurse from the third floor and a teacher with a cello from the second floor. Together. If they want.”

For a long time Mara couldn't say anything. She stood in the middle of the empty room, where she had drunk tea and taken blood pressure every Wednesday for four years, where she had read out the letter from 1961, where Grete had played Chopin for her. Then she said: “I have to talk to Jakob.” Ludwig nodded. “Of course. Let me know. But not too late. You know: no lost years.” That evening, Mara let him know. Jakob hadn't hesitated for a second.

On the first Sunday in March, Andrei, Piotr and Jakob carried the furniture from two flats up to the fourth floor. This time not a grand piano, but a cello, two beds that became one and an awful lot of books. When everything was upstairs, Jakob put his cello exactly where the three round marks were in the wooden floor. “So that the spot isn't left empty,” he said. In the evening at nine he opened the window and played. And two streets away, at the care home, people said later, an old lady had sat in the garden and smiled, as if she had heard.
